prompt.context: Mayor Bloomberg has asked you to come to NYC as a Diamond consultant and advise him on whether Wi-Fi should be accessible to all of Manhattan free of charge. The Mayor has looked at several studies and has seen some research on economic impact.
prompt.question: What would you consider and investigate in order to determine whether the Mayor should or should not make Wi-Fi free and accessible to all of Manhattan?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any financial constraints or a budget ceiling for this initiative?
clarifying_info.a: No specific budget has been set yet; that is part of what we need to determine.

clarifying_info.q: Is this limited to outdoor public spaces or would it include residential coverage?
clarifying_info.a: The intent is citywide coverage across all of Manhattan.

clarifying_info.q: Has any city already implemented a similar model?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, there are other cities that have attempted or implemented free municipal Wi-Fi — benchmarking them is encouraged.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the potential providers or operators of this Wi-Fi network?
clarifying_info.a: That is an open question to explore — the city could partner with private providers or fund it directly.

framework: Level 1 — Usefulness to the population: assess current Internet access rates and diagnose why people lack access (supply-side gaps vs. demand-side disinterest).
Level 2 — Impact on existing for-profit Internet providers: identify affected players and the customer segments they would lose.

Level 3 — Revenue loss estimation for affected providers: size the subscribing population across households, businesses, and academic institutions; consider who might actually benefit from free access.

Level 4 — Advantages, caveats, and alternatives: benchmark other cities, evaluate technology choices, assess risk of capital investment becoming obsolete, explore alternative delivery models, and flag security/privacy/speed concerns.
Level 5 — Implementation: estimate total cost and determine who bears it.

questions.prompt: Level 1 — Would this implementation be useful to the population? Walk through the demand analysis.
questions.guidance: Candidate should split the population into those with and without current Internet access. Among the unconnected, distinguish supply-side barriers (service gaps, pricing, slow speeds) from demand-side barriers (no computer, no perceived value, age demographics). This segmentation determines whether free Wi-Fi actually closes the gap or misses the real problem.

questions.prompt: Level 2 — How would free municipal Wi-Fi affect existing for-profit Internet providers?
questions.guidance: Candidate should name relevant incumbents (Comcast, Time Warner Cable, Verizon FiOS, etc.), then map which customer segments each serves. The key insight is that these businesses would face direct revenue cannibalization if their paying customers switch to free city Wi-Fi.

questions.prompt: Level 3 — Estimate the revenue loss to affected providers by sizing the subscribing population.
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment current subscribers into three buckets: (1) households, (2) businesses, and (3) academic institutions (schools and universities). For each, consider whether they might actually benefit from free access (e.g., schools with tight budgets). The candidate should then reason about how to justify the decision to existing providers — potential compensation, partnerships, or phased implementation. No specific calculation is required; the case tests structuring ability.

questions.prompt: Level 4 — What are the advantages and key risks/caveats of this decision?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: (a) positive economic and social impact, supported by benchmarking cities that have tried municipal Wi-Fi; (b) technology choice — is Wi-Fi the best option vs. DSL, cable, or other broadband; (c) alternative delivery mechanisms (subsidizing access for specific populations, kiosks, Internet cafes, expanded public library access); (d) technology obsolescence risk — capital invested in Wi-Fi infrastructure could be devalued if technology evolves; (e) practical concerns: security, privacy, and speed/reliability.

questions.prompt: Level 5 — How would implementation work, and who pays?
questions.guidance: Candidate should address: total capital and operating cost estimate (even high-level order-of-magnitude), funding sources (city budget, public-private partnership, federal grants, ISP cost-sharing), and whether stakeholders — taxpayers, businesses, ISPs — would agree to bear the cost. A strong candidate ties cost-sharing back to Level 3 findings about who benefits.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternative ways could the city provide broad Internet access to underserved Manhattan residents, other than a free citywide Wi-Fi network?

categories.name: Infrastructure alternatives
ideas: Subsidized DSL or cable for low-income households
City-funded fiber build-out to underserved neighborhoods
Public-private partnership with ISPs to expand coverage at reduced rates

categories.name: Shared-access models
ideas: Expanded public library Internet terminals and hours
Internet kiosks in subway stations, parks, and community centers
Internet cafes with city subsidies in low-income areas

categories.name: Device and digital-literacy support
ideas: Subsidized device programs (laptops, tablets) for households without computers
Digital literacy training programs to address demand-side barriers
School-based community Internet access programs after hours

categories.name: Targeted subsidies
ideas: Means-tested Internet vouchers redeemable with any ISP
Subsidizing access only for academic institutions and schools
Corporate sponsorship of free Wi-Fi in high-traffic commercial corridors

recommendation: Based on the five-level analysis, the Mayor should pursue free Manhattan Wi-Fi only if: the majority of unconnected residents face supply-side (not demand-side) barriers, existing providers can be compensated or partnered with to offset revenue loss, and total implementation cost is within a range the city and private partners can jointly fund.

If demand-side barriers (lack of devices, digital literacy, perceived value) dominate, free Wi-Fi will not meaningfully close the access gap, and targeted subsidies or alternative delivery models would generate higher impact per dollar.
risks: Technology obsolescence — Wi-Fi infrastructure invested today may be superseded before ROI is realized.
ISP opposition — incumbents may lobby against or legally challenge the initiative.
Security and privacy vulnerabilities on an open public network.
Underutilization if device ownership and digital literacy gaps are not addressed simultaneously.
Cost overruns during citywide infrastructure deployment.
next_steps: Commission a detailed survey of unconnected Manhattan residents to quantify supply-side vs. demand-side access barriers.
Benchmark 3-5 cities (e.g., Philadelphia, San Francisco) that have attempted municipal Wi-Fi to assess outcomes and cost structures.
Engage Comcast, Time Warner Cable, and Verizon FiOS in preliminary partnership discussions to explore revenue-sharing or co-investment models.
Issue an RFP for network design and cost estimation to determine total capital and operating expenditure.
Pilot free Wi-Fi in one underserved neighborhood before committing to full Manhattan rollout.
